And this was a symbol of the fact that some of your nation would be found children of Abraham, and found, too, in the lot of Christ; but that others, who are indeed children of Abraham, would be like the sand on the sea-shore, barren and fruitless, much in quantity, and without number indeed, but bearing no fruit whatever, and only drinking the water of the sea.

The Lord conferring with Isaac, after saying other things, proceeds —

[Passage quoted, Gen. xxvi. 3.]

Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was born of the seed of Isaac, according to the flesh, in Whom all the nations of the earth are blessed, in learning through Him of Almighty God, and in being taught through Him to bless men dear to God. So there is reciprocal blessing, they enjoying the same blessing as the men they bless, according to God's saying to Abraham : " Blessed be they that bless thee."
26:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 1

26:4.t: Moreover, the example that has been taken from Genesis is contained thus in its own book: "And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" (Gen. 26:4). Interpreting this of Christ, the Apostle says: "It is not written 'of seeds,' as in many, but as in one, 'and your seed,' which is Christ". And this we ought to observe in almost all the testimonies that have been taken from the old books into the New Testament: that the evangelists or apostles trusted to memory, and, setting out only the sense, often changed the order, and sometimes either took words away or added them. But no one doubts that it was not in Isaac and Jacob, or in the twelve patriarchs, and the others who descend from the stock of Abraham, that all the nations were blessed, but in Christ Jesus, through whom all the Gentiles praise God, and a new name is blessed upon the earth.

26:5.t:
And Abraham himself, coming later than those already named, being younger than they according to the age men reached in those times, though an old man in reality, was the first to receive circumcision as a seal, for the sake of his descendants, and he left it to those who should be born of him according to the flesh as a sign of their descent from him. He too before he had a son, and before he was circumcised, by his rejection of idolatry, and his confession of the one omnipotent God, yea, by his virtuous life alone is shown to be one who lived as a Christian, not as a Jew. For he is represented as having kept the commandments and the precepts and the ordinances of God before the enactments of Moses. That is why God giving the oracle to Isaac says:

"And I will give to thy seed all this land, and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. Because Abraham thy father heard my voice, and kept my commandments, and my laws, and my judgments, and my statutes." […]
26:5.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 6

26:5.t: Isaac is a patriarch who had no second wife, nor any concubine, but was content with the twins who were the fruit of a single intercourse. He too had the same fears as his father of the perilous beauty of his wife when he lived among strangers, and he too called her sister without a word about her being his wife, since in fact she was nearly related on the paternal and the maternal side. And Rebekah too was safe, once it was known that she was his wife. Not, however, that we should esteem him higher than his father for knowing no woman other than his single wife; undoubtedly the merits of his father's faith and obedience were so much greater that it was because of the father that God was so good to the son.

26:7.t: Those who assert that sometimes we must lie make inappropriate mention of Abraham as having lied about Sarah whom he called his sister. For he did not say "She is not my wife" but "She is my sister," because Sarah was in fact of a family so closely related that without lying she could be called his sister. This fact Abraham confirmed afterward when Sarah was returned by him who had led her away. Abraham replied to him, saying, "Also she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother," that is to say, belonging to his father's family but not to his mother's. Thus he concealed something of the truth but did not say anything false in concealing the fact that she was his wife and in saying that she was his sister. His son Isaac also did this, for we know that he too chose a relative of his as wife. Hence it is not a lie when truth is passed over in silence but when falsehood is brought forth in speech.

26:8.t: Isaac means "rejoicing." The inquisitive king saw him playing with his wife and helpmate, Rebekah. The king (his name was Abimelech) represents, I believe, a wisdom above this world, looking down upon the mystery signified by such childlike playing. Rebekah means "submission." Oh, what prudent playing! Rejoicing joined to submission, with the king as audience. The Spirit exults in such merrymaking in Christ, attended with submissiveness. This is in truth godly childlikeness.…It is possible to interpret the meaning of the inspired Word in still another sense: that it refers to our rejoicing and making merry because of our salvation, like Isaac's. He rejoiced because he had been saved from death; that is why he played and rejoiced with his spouse, as we with our helpmate in salvation, the church. […]

26:12.t: After these things it says "Isaac sowed barley, and found a hundredfold. And the Lord blessed him, and the man was magnified, and by his advance he became greater, until he became exceedingly great." What is this, that Isaac "sowed barley" and not wheat, and is blessed in that he sows "barley" and is magnified, "until he becomes great"? It appears therefore that he was not yet great, but after he "sowed barley" and gathered "a hundredfold," then "he became exceedingly great." Barley is especially the food of beasts of burden or of country slaves. For it is a rougher kind, and one which seems to prick the one touching it as if with certain points. Isaac is the word of God, which word in the law sows barley, in the Gospels wheat. For it prepares that food for the more perfect and spiritual, this for the more unskilled and animal, because it is written: "men and beasts you will save, O Lord." Isaac therefore, the word of the law, sows barley, and nevertheless in that very barley finds "a hundredfold fruit." […]

And the full and perfect number is in the number of ten decades, which also multiplies the sowing of Isaac with a hundredfold crop; but because he was on earth and could still say: I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were, he is related to have sown barley and reaped a hundredfold crop: for the grain of wheat had not yet died in the earth, to bear many fruits and to satisfy the Jewish people's hunger for hearing the word of God with that bread which came down from heaven; but how the hundred cubits were not only toward the eastern gate but also toward the gate of the north, the following testimony will show.

And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that year a hundredfold of barley. Although Isaac sowed in a foreign land, still I do not think that he had so great a fertility of barley. Hence I think that is better which is found in the Hebrew, and which Aquila also translated, and he found in that year a hundredfold reckoned, that is, ἑκατὸν εἰκασμούς. For although 'estimation' and 'barley' are written with the same letters, yet estimations are read saarim, but barleys sorim. And Scripture, by keeping silent about the kind of crop that was multiplied a hundredfold, seems to me to have shown the multiplication of all virtues in him. Accordingly there follows: [Gen 26:13] and the Lord blessed him, and the man became great, and he walked on, going and magnified, until he became exceedingly great. But I do not know whether the good fortune of multiplied barley could make anyone glorious.

26:13.t: But after this "the Lord," it says, "blessed Isaac, and he became exceedingly great." Isaac was small in the law, but by the advance of time he becomes great. He becomes great by the advance of time in the prophets. For when he is in the law alone, he is not yet great, seeing that it is also covered with a veil. He grows therefore already in the prophets; but when he has come even to this, that he casts off the veil also, then he will be "exceedingly great." When the letter of the law begins to be separated out like the chaff of its barley, and it appears that "the law is spiritual," then Isaac will be magnified and will become "exceedingly great." For see that in the Gospels also the Lord breaks a few loaves, and how many thousands of peoples He refreshes "and how many baskets" of leftovers remain over. So long as the loaves are whole, no one is filled, no one is refreshed, nor do the loaves themselves seem to be increased. […]

Do you wish to know how "increase" is to be understood? Hear what Isaac did, of whom it is said: "Isaac went forward and became greater, until he became great, or exceedingly great indeed". For his will, ever stretching itself toward better things, had its advances, his mind contemplated something more divine, and he exercised himself in memory, so as to store up more things in his treasury and retain them more firmly. And in this manner it comes about that whoever has cultivated all his virtues in the field of his soul fulfills the commandment enjoining: "increase".
26:13.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 11

26:15.t: There are, then, wells which the servants of Abraham dug, but these the Philistines had filled with earth. These, therefore, Isaac first sets about to cleanse. The Philistines hate waters, they love earth; Isaac loves waters, he always seeks wells, he cleanses the old, he opens the new. Behold our Isaac, who "was offered as a victim for us," coming into the valley of Gerar, which is interpreted as "a wall" or "a hedge"—coming, I say, that he might "break down the middle wall of the hedge, the enmities in his flesh"—coming to take away the wall, that is, sin, which separates between us and God, the wall which stands between us and the heavenly powers, that he might make "both one" and carry back the sheep that had strayed "upon his shoulders" to the mountains and restore it to the other "ninety-nine that had not strayed." This Isaac, then, our Savior, when he had come into that valley of Gerar, wills first of all to dig those wells which the servants of his father had dug; […]

26:17.t: And Isaac went away from there and came into the valley of Gerar and dwelt there. In place of 'valley' it has 'torrent' in the Hebrew. For Isaac, after he had been magnified, could not dwell in a valley. But he dwelt at the torrent of which it is written, he drinks of the torrent in the way, from which Elijah too drank in the time of famine. But because Elijah was not perfect as Christ is, that torrent therefore dried up for him. But our Lord too was betrayed at a torrent, consecrating our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.

26:18.t: I think this same thing is signified also by what is in Genesis, that wells are dug by the servants of Isaac which had been made by Abraham and which the Philistines had stopped up with earth. As long as Abraham lives, his wells are not closed; but when he is dead and the wells are stopped up, if servants dig, the Philistines oppose them, and there is strife. But if Isaac himself comes and digs a well and finds water, the Philistines have no power to oppose him. See Peter and Paul, and you will not doubt about the wells and rivers of Christ.

26:19.t: We find that the exercises of the Patriarchs concerning wells are always the customary ones. For behold, Scripture relates that Isaac, after "the Lord blessed him and he was made exceedingly great," undertook a great work. And he began, it says, to dig wells, "the wells which his father Abraham's servants had dug in the time of his father Abraham, but the Philistines had stopped them up and filled them with earth." First, then, "he dwelt by the well of vision," and, illumined by the well of vision, he set about opening other wells—and not first new wells, but those that his father Abraham had dug. And when he had dug the first well, "the Philistines," it says, "envied him." Yet he was not frightened by their envy nor did he yield to their spite, but "again," it says, "he dug the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, and which the Philistines had stopped up after the death of his father Abraham; and he gave them names according to the names his father had given them." […]

For Abraham dug wells and Isaac too—that is, the mighty patriarchs—and Jacob also, as we find in the Gospel, as if they were fountains of the human race, and specifically fountains of faith and devotion. For what is a well of living water but a depth of profound instruction? On this account Hagar saw the angel by a well and Jacob found his wife Rachel by a well; Moses too earned the first rewards of his future marriage beside a well. Therefore Isaac undertook to open wells out of a depth of vision and in good order, so that the water of his well might first wash and strengthen the reasoning faculty of the soul and its eye, to make its sight clearer.
26:19.s: On Isaac and the Soul, Chapter 4, Sections 21-22

26:19.t: And the servants of Isaac dug in the valley of Gerar, and found there a well of living water. Here too 'torrent' is written in place of 'valley'. For a well of living water is never found in a valley.

26:21.t: And they dug another well, and they quarrelled over it also: and he called its name Enmities. In place of 'enmities', which Aquila and Symmachus translated τὴν ἀντικειμένην and ἐναντίωσιν, that is, the adverse and the contrary, in the Hebrew it has satanan. From this we understand that satanan means 'contrary'.

26:22.t: After this, then, Isaac digs a third well and "called the name of that place 'breadth,' saying: because now the Lord has enlarged us and increased us upon the earth." For truly now Isaac has been enlarged, and his name has been increased over all the earth, since he has fulfilled in us the knowledge of the Trinity. For then only "in Judea was God known" and in Israel his name was named, but now "into all the earth their sound has gone forth, and their words unto the ends of the world." For Isaac's servants, going forth throughout the whole world, dug wells and showed "living water" to all, "baptizing all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." For "the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." But each one of us also, who ministers the word of God, digs a well and seeks "living water," from which to refresh his hearers. […]

If, therefore, you too, hearing these things today, receive the hearing faithfully, Isaac works also in you, he cleanses your hearts from earthly senses, and, seeing that such great mysteries as these lie hidden in the divine scriptures, you advance in understanding, you advance in spiritual senses. You will begin even yourselves to be teachers, and "rivers of living water" will proceed from you. For the Word of God is present, and this now is his operation, that he may remove the earth from the soul of each one of you and open your fountain. For he is within you and does not come from without, just as "the kingdom of God also is within you." And that woman who had lost the drachma did not find it outside, but in her own house, after she "lit a lamp and cleansed the house" of the filth and uncleannesses which the sloth and dullness of long time had heaped up, and there she found the drachma. […]

Now Isaac reopened many wells that his father had dug, but strangers had filled them after the death of his father Abraham. Beyond the others he dug the following wells: one in the valley of Gerar, and he found there a well of living water; and the shepherds of Gerar disputed with Isaac's shepherds, because they claimed the water of this well as their own, and he called its name "Injustice." And he dug another well over which a quarrel arose, and he called it "Enmity." And he dug a third well, over which no dispute began among the shepherds, and he called it "Room Enough." He also dug a well and did not find water in it and called that well "Well of the Oath." Would anyone reading of these things consider that those works were earthly rather than spiritual?
26:22.s: On Isaac and the Soul, Chapter 4, Sections 20-21

26:22.t: And they dug another well: and they did not strive with them, and he called its name Breadth. In place of 'breadth' in the Hebrew it has rooboth, which proves what we said above, he built the city of Nineveh and rooboth, that is, its streets.

26:23.t: It is written in the prophet, speaking in the person of the Lord: "and in the hands of the prophets I was made like." This saying indicates that, although our Lord Jesus Christ is one according to his substance and is nothing other than the Son of God, nevertheless in the figures and forms of the Scriptures he is displayed as varied and diverse. For example, as I recall we set forth in earlier passages that he himself was in the type of Isaac, when he was being offered for a holocaust, yet he himself also held the form of the ram. I say further that he is also displayed in the angel who spoke to Abraham and says to him: "do not lay your hand upon the boy" — since again he says to him: "because you have done this thing, in blessing I will bless you." He is called the sheep or the lamb that is sacrificed at the Passover, and he himself is signified as the shepherd of the sheep; and the high priest who offers the sacrifice is nonetheless described as he himself. […]

"Isaac therefore went up to the well of the oath, and the Lord appeared to him." The going up of the Law we have said even before to be the ornament of the temple and of those divine services which were performed there. The increase of the prophets too can be named a going up of the Law; and for that reason perhaps he is said to have gone up to the well of the oath and there the Lord to have appeared to him. For through the prophets "the Lord swore, and will not repent, that he himself is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." "At the well" therefore "of the oath" God was seen by him, confirming the promises to come upon him.

26:25.t: "And Isaac built there an altar, and called upon the name of the Lord, and pitched there his tent. And the servants of Isaac dug there a well." Isaac indeed builds an altar even in the Law and pitches his tent; but in the Gospels he does not pitch a tent, but builds a house and lays a foundation. For hear Wisdom saying of the Church: "wisdom," it says, "built herself a house, and set up seven columns." Hear also Paul saying of this: "for no one can lay a foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus." Where therefore there is a tent, even if it be pitched, without doubt it must be dissolved; but where there are foundations and the house is built "upon the rock," that house is never dissolved, "for it has been founded upon the rock." Nevertheless Isaac there too digs a well, and never ceases from digging wells, until there arises "a fountain of living water" and "the rush of the river gladdens the city of God."

26:26.t: But "Abimelech" also (he who long ago had honored Abraham) now "came" with his friends "from Gerar" to Isaac: "and Isaac says to them: why have you come to me? For you have hated me and cast me out from you. To this they answer: seeing," it says, "we have seen that the Lord is with you, and we said: let there be an oath between us and you, and let us establish a covenant with you, that you do no evil with us," and the rest. This Abimelech, as I see it, does not always have peace with Isaac, but sometimes is at variance, sometimes seeks peace. If you remember how we said in earlier passages about Abimelech that he holds the person of the studious and wise of the world, who through the learning of philosophy have grasped many things even from the truth, you can understand how here with Isaac, who holds the figure of the Word of God which is in the Law, he can neither be always in dissension nor always in peace. For philosophy is neither in all things contrary to the Law of God nor in all things in agreement. […]

And Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ochozath his groomsman, and Phicol the chief of his soldiery. In place of 'Ochozath his groomsman' in the Hebrew it has the company of his friends, so that it signifies not so much a man as the crowd of friends that had come with the king, among whom was also Phicol, the chief of his army.

26:30.t: But what do they ask? "Do not do," they say, "evils with us; but as we have not cursed you, so also may you be blessed of the Lord." They seem to me through these words to be demanding remission of sins, that they may not receive evils. They ask for a blessing, not for retribution. Finally, see what follows. "And Isaac made for them," it says, "a great feast: and they ate and drank." For it is certain that he who ministers the word "is a debtor to the wise and the unwise." Since therefore here he provides a feast for the wise, for that reason it is said that he made not a small, but a "great feast." And you too, if you are not yet a "little one" and in need of "milk," but bring "practised senses" and, with much learning sent ahead, come more capable for the understanding of the word of God, a "great feast" is made for you too. […]

Let us imitate Isaac's goodness; let us imitate his purity. Isaac was certainly a good and virtuous man, devoted to God and faithful to his wife. He did not return evil for evil. He yielded to those who drove him out, but he received them again when they were sorry, being neither harsh to insolence nor obdurate to kindness. When he went away from others, he fled to avoid strife. When he received them again, he readily forgave them, and he was exceptionally kind when he pardoned. Men sought to associate with him, and he added a delightful feast.
26:30.s: On the Decease of His Brother Satyrus, Book 2, Section 99

26:32.t: And the servants of Isaac came and told him of the well which they had dug, and said to him, We have found water, and he called its name Fullness. I do not know how it comes to be found in the Seventy translators, and the servants of Isaac came and told him of the well which they had dug, and said to him, We have not found water: and he called its name Oath. For what ἐτυμολογία [etymology] is it for it to be called 'oath' because they had not found water? On the contrary, in the Hebrew, with whose rendering Aquila and Symmachus also agree, it signifies this: that they found water, and that for this reason the well itself was named Fullness and the city called Bersabee, that is, the well of fullness. […]

27:1.t: IF THE WILL OF THE RIGHTEOUS MAN IS GOOD, WHY DID NOT ISAAC BLESS ESAU AS HE WISHED, BUT JACOB WHOM HE WOULD NOT BLESS? — The righteous man’s will is good, as far as his own conscience is concerned; but with respect to foreknowledge, it is free from opposing events. For God alone is the one who judges things to come. Therefore Isaac, righteous as to his present human understanding, considered his elder son more worthy to receive the blessing. But God, who is the knower of hidden things, showed that the younger deserved the blessing, so that in the blessing He might show the benefit to be not from man, but from God; for the dignity of the office, not the merit of the man, is what God’s blessing follows. Accordingly, it was said by God in Numbers to Moses and Aaron the priests, You shall place my name upon the children of Israel; I, the Lord, will bless them (Num. […]
27:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 11: WHY ISAAC BLESSED JACOB AND NOT ESAU

27:5.t:
While Esau was delayed in hunting, so that he might bring his father food from wild animals and thereby receive a blessing from him, the mother brought Jacob to his father to receive the blessing; for while the Jewish people were devoted to the observances of the Law and came more slowly to the reception of faith in Christ, the mother, grace, offered the people of the nations to God to receive the blessing that was owed to the Jews, because they had embraced faith in Christ with eagerness. How the very people of the nations merited this gift of blessing is attested in figure by the deeds of Jacob, which are described as having been done in order to receive the blessing.

So Rebecca said to her son Jacob: Bring me two of the best young goats, and I will make from them dishes for your father, such as he likes to eat; and he will bless you before the Lord, before he dies (Gen. 27:9). He went and brought them, and gave them to his mother. […]

27:11.t: Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Where we read 'hairy', in the Hebrew it is written seir. Hence afterwards the region of Mount Seir, in which he lived, was so called: we have spoken of this above as well.

And that no man may imagine that his simplicity was natural foolishness, see how attentive he was to the curses of his father, and how he returned answer concerning the things which were set forth by knowledge, "Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Peradventure my father will feel me, and I shall be in his eyes as a mocker, and curses shall come upon me and not blessings." But his mother in faith, being certain of those early promises which were revealed to her, made answer unto him, saying, "Upon me be thy curses, my son, only hear my voice, and do what I command thee;" and straightway he was obedient to his mother like a child.
27:11.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

27:15.t: Accordingly Jacob received his brother's clothing, because he excelled the elder in wisdom. Thus the younger brother took the clothing of the elder because he was conspicuous in the merit of his faith. Rebekah presented this clothing as a symbol of the church; she gave to the younger son the clothing of the Old Testament, the prophetic and priestly clothing, the royal Davidic clothing, the clothing of the kings Solomon and Hezekiah and Josiah. She gave it too to the Christian people, who would know how to use the garment they had received, since the Jewish people kept it without using it and did not know its proper adornments. This clothing was lying in shadow, cast off and forgotten; it was tarnished by a dark haze of impiety and could not be unfolded further in their confined hearts. The Christian people put it on, and it shone brightly. They made it bright with the splendor of their faith and the light of their holy works. Isaac recognized the familiar fragrance that attached to his people. […]
27:15.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 2, Section 9

27:15.t: And Rebecca took the garments of Esau her elder son, which were precious, with her at home. In this place too the Hebrews relate that the firstborn performed the office of priests and had a priestly garment, clothed in which they offered victims to God, before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

But by the delightful foods that were prepared for Isaac to be taken from the two kids, we must understand works of penance. John the Baptist speaks of these foods when he says: “Produce fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8). By the very fine garments, however, which Esau, that is, the Jews, had left at home, we can understand the excellent teachings of the Law, such as this one: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6:5), and many others, without which no one can be righteous. These are the finest garments which the Jews left at home, that is, in the Old Testament, because they were unwilling to observe them. Clothed and adorned with these, the Gentile people went to God the Father with the food of good works. And together with the foods he also brought breads. […]

27:16.t: And this was clearly shown of Rahab of Jericho, and the patriarch Jacob; the former of whom could only escape death by means of this remedy, while the latter could not secure the blessing of the first-born without it. For God is not only the Judge and inspector of our words and actions, but He also looks into their purpose and aim. And if He sees that anything has been done or promised by some one for the sake of eternal salvation and shows insight into Divine contemplation, even though it may appear to men to be hard and unfair, yet He looks at the inner goodness of the heart and regards the desire of the will rather than the actual words spoken, because He must take into account the aim of the work and the disposition of the doer, whereby, as was said above, one man may be justified by means of a lie, while another may be guilty of a sin of everlasting death by telling the truth. […]
27:16.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 17

27:19.t: Joseph: In every case, as we said, we must look not at the progress of the work but at the intention of the worker, nor must we inquire to begin with what a man has done, but with what purpose, so that we may find that some have been condemned for those deeds from which good has afterwards arisen, andon the other hand that some have arrived by means of acts in themselves reprehensible at the height of righteousness. And in the case of the former the good result of their actions was of no avail to them as they took the matter in and with an evil purpose, and wanted to bring about-not the good which actually resulted, but something of the opposite character; nor was the bad beginning injurious to the latter, as he put up with the necessity of a blameworthy start; not out of disregard for God, or with the purpose of doing wrong, but with an eye to a needful and holy end. […]
27:19.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapters 11-12

27:25.t: Now although this meat is a burden unto the wise and prudent, yet was it given by promise unto Noah, and it was sent unto Elijah in a gift, and Abraham received God and His angels thereby, and Isaac was pleased to pour out blessings upon Jacob thereby, and Samuel offered this gift beforehand to Saul as to a king, and David and all the righteous kings made use of such meat, and it was employed by all the righteous; and they were not blamed therefor, because they were superior to lust. And they did not eat like slaves with lust, but they made use of every thing with authority like free men.

After Isaac had taken food, Jacob also offered him wine. If the works of the active life are signified by food, we can understand by wine, which alienates the minds of men, the contemplative life, which renders the minds of certain of the elect insensitive to love of the world. Therefore, after food and drink had been taken, Isaac blessed Jacob; for those receive the blessing of the heavenly homeland from God who strive to please him with good works until the end of their life.

27:27.t: Flowers, too, I have, more blooming and lasting than all those of spring, "out of the full land that the Lord hath blessed," that is, the holy and sweet-smelling pastors and teachers, and all that is pure and choice of the congregation; with these do I desire to be crowned and to go in procession, "having fought the good fight, having finished my course, having kept the faith," according to the holy Apostle.

For of him it is written, "Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field." He had been made perfect in virtue's every flower and was fragrant with the grace of the holy blessing and of the happiness of heaven. He is indeed the field that the Lord has blessed. [This field is] not the earthly field with its rugged woods and crashing torrents, its swampy, sluggish waters, unproductive grain lands, and barren vineyards, filled with sterile rock and gravel, pockmarked and arid with drought or wet with blood, and choked over with brambles and thorns, but the field of which the church speaks in the Canticle, "I have adjured you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and virtues of the field." This is the field of which the Lord also says, "With me is the beauty of the field." In this field the grape is found that was pressed and poured out blood and washed the world clean. In this field is the fig tree, and beneath it the saints will find rest and be renewed by a good and spiritual grace. […]
27:27.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 1, Section 3

27:27.t: And so Jacob was fragrant with the fragrance of such fruits; he followed God amid dangers and believed that he was safe everywhere, led by the Lord. Although the fragrance of the field is pleasant and sweet because it is a natural fragrance, still there breathed in the holy patriarch the fragrance of grace and virtue. How moderate and restrained he was! He did not claim the food that had been prepared for him but yielded without delay to his brother's request for it and received from him the birthright of the firstborn. How respectful he was toward his parents! Through his mother's love he earned the preference over his elder brother, and through the gift of his father's blessing he was made holy. How respectful of God's commands he was! He refused to do wrong to his brother. How honorable! He resisted practicing deceit upon his father. How respectful! He could not refuse his mother what she ordered.
27:27.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 1, Section 4

27:27.t: This dew is the influence of the Holy Spirit's grace which visits the Scriptures and in which it is sweetly found. Hence, in Genesis: "The fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed! God give you dew from heaven, and fruitfulness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine." Jacob, that spiritual man, is well learned in the Sacred Scriptures. Out of him comes forth an odor that abounds throughout the Scriptures in their threefold meaning: the grain referring to allegory, the wine to tropology, and the oil to anagogy.

27:28.t: We find that Isaac also, blessing Jacob, says: "May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine". Do you suppose that Isaac was giving in blessing to his son Jacob such grain as sinful men also have, and with which even the impious Pharaoh abounded? Was this the blessing of so great a patriarch? Do you wish that I still show you how others also, the unjust, have a multitude of grain? Behold that man in the Gospel, whose "field brought forth many fruits, who says": "I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; eat, drink, and be merry". Do we therefore believe such to be the goods which by divine blessings were handed over to the saints and to the faithful? Other fruits of the earth do I behold, and otherwise do I regard the multitude of "birth". […]

27:29.t: He is not a slave, it is said; not a master, but free. Oh the terrible insensibility, the pitiable audacity, of them that maintain this! Shall I rather lament in them their ignorance or their blasphemy? They try to insult the doctrines that concern the divine nature by comparing them with the human, and endeavour to apply to the ineffable nature of God that common custom of human life whereby the difference of degrees is variable, not perceiving that among men no one is a slave by nature. For men are either brought under a yoke of slavery by conquest, as when prisoners are taken in war; or they are enslaved on account of poverty, as the Egyptians were oppressed by Pharaoh; or, by a wise and mysterious dispensation, the worst children are by their fathers' order condemned to serve the wiser and the better; and this any righteous enquirer into the circumstances would declare to be not a sentence of condemnation but a benefit. […]

Let peoples serve thee, and let their princes bow down to thee, and be thou Lord over thy brethren, and let thy father's sons bow down to thee; cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be every one that blesseth thee. But we see not all these things accomplished upon Jacob, but see rather that Jacob, having prostrated himself seven times upon the ground, made obeisance to Esau. And thirty kings, sprung from Esau, reigned before ever a king reigned in Israel; so that these blessings await Him who was expected to descend from them, namely, the Lord Christ, whom the whole scope of divine scripture has in view.

27:30.t: Afterward, when the blessing had been pronounced, the elder brother arrived. By this it is revealed that the kingdom was predestined to be bestowed on the church rather than on the synagogue but had secretly entered the synagogue so that sin might abound, and, when sin had abounded, that grace might also abound. At the same time, it would be clear that the candidate for the kingdom of heaven must be quick to carry off the blessing and to appropriate the prerogative for which he has been recommended. On this account the younger son was not blamed by his father but praised, for Isaac says, "Your brother came deceitfully and received your blessing." For deceit is good when the plunder is without reproach. Now the plunder of piety is without reproach, because "from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away." […]
27:30.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 3, Section 10

27:36.t: And Esau said, Justly was his name called Jacob, for behold, he has supplanted me a second time. Jacob means 'supplanter'. So from the fact that he deceived his brother by craft, he alluded to the name of him who was called Jacob before for this reason, that at his birth he had grasped his brother's heel.

Now this is the first lust which conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the law took place. It dismissed from Esau his birthright and his blessings. For the lust of the belly is the captain of the host of the left side, and to it are fettered all the hosts of sin, and as captains of hosts go forth to war at the head of their companies against the enemy, even so also doth it, as the captain of the host of all wickedness, go forth to war against that which is good.

27:40.t: For first, He gave the Kingdom to the sons of Jacob, and subdued to them the children of Esau; as Isaac said to Esau:—Thou shalt serve Jacob thy brother. And when again they did not prosper in the Kingdom, He took it away from the children of Jacob and gave it to the children of Esau until He should come Whose it is. And they will deliver up the deposit to its Giver, and will not deal fraudulently with it.

Nevertheless Esau brought it about by his demands and entreaties that he did receive a blessing but such a blessing as was in agreement and correspondence with the earlier one, namely, that he should serve his brother. Indeed, the one who could not command and rule the other ought to have served him, in order to be ruled by the one who was wiser. It was not the role of the holy patriarch to deliver his own son to the ignoble state of slavery. But since he had two sons, one without moderation and the other moderate and wise, in order to take care for both like a good father, he placed the moderate son over the immediate one, and he ordered the foolish one to obey the one who was wise. For the foolish man cannot of his own accord be a disciple of virtue or persevere in his intent, because the fool changes like the moon. Isaac was right to deny Esau freedom to make his own choices; else he might drift like a ship in the waves without a helmsman. […]
27:40.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 3, Section 11

27:40.t: Everyone who does not possess the authority conferred by a clear conscience is a slave; whoever is crushed by fear or ensnared by pleasure or seduced by desires or provoked by wrath or felled by grief is a slave. In fact, every passion is servile, because "everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin," and, what is worse, he is the slave of many sins. The person who is subject to vices has sold himself to many masters, so that he is scarcely permitted to go out of servitude. But take the one who is the master over his own will, judge over his counsels, agent of his judgment, the man who restrains the longing of his bodily passions and does well what he does. (Note that by acting well he acts rightly, and one who acts rightly acts without blame or reproach because he has power over his actions.) Such a person is assuredly free. For the one who does all things wisely and in complete accord with his will is the only free man. It is not accidental status that makes the slave but shameful and foolish conduct. […]
27:40.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 3, Section 12

27:40.t: This then is what the patriarch Isaac says, "You shall serve your brother. But the time will be, when you shall shake off and loose his yoke from your neck." He means that there will be two peoples, one the son of the slave girl, the other of the free woman—for the letter is a slave, whereas grace is free16—and that the people that attends to the letter is going to be a slave as long as it needs to follow the expounder of learning in the spirit. Then that will also come to pass which the apostle says, "that the remnant may be saved by reason of the election made by grace." "You shall serve your brother," but then you will perceive your advancement in servitude only when you begin to obey your brother voluntarily and not under compulsion.
27:40.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 3, Section 13

27:40.t: And you shall serve your brother: and the time shall be when you shall put off and loose his yoke from your neck. It signifies that the Idumaeans would serve the Jews, and that the time would come when they would throw off the yoke of servitude from their neck and resist their rule. But according to the Seventy translators, who said, but it shall be, when you have put off and loosed the yoke from your neck, the sentence seems to hang and not to be complete.

27:41.t: But we shouldn't leave his parents without excuse for having preferred their younger son to the elder. At the same time we must take care so that no one, in turning to their example, would make an unfair judgment between his sons or suppose that he should love the one and esteem the other less. From this line of conduct fraternal hatreds are aroused and the crime of fratricide is contrived to gain a worthless sum of money. Let children be nurtured with an equal measure of devotion. Granted that one's love may fasten more upon some trait in a child who is more agreeable or similar to oneself, the exercise of justice ought to be the same in regard to all. The more that is given to the child that is loved and who seeks his brother's love, the more is taken away from the one who is burdened with jealousy at the unfair preferment. Esau threatened that he would kill his brother. […]
27:41.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 2, Sections 5-6

27:42.t: But falsehood cannot seize those who flee from the Judea of the letter to the spiritual and intelligible things and the sublime mountains of truth. And that we may understand let them flee into the mountains, take as an example what is said manifestly of a praiseworthy flight, such as what the Apostle says: "flee fornication", and what Wisdom says: "as from the face of a serpent, flee sin", or such as what Rebecca says to Jacob in a mystery: "behold, Esau thy brother threatens to kill thee. Now therefore, my son, hear my voice, and rising up flee to Laban my brother in Haran; and dwell with him some days, until the wrath of thy brother be turned away". And everyone (I think) who is a son of Jacob, completing the works of Jacob, understanding every disposition hateful to God, which is Esau, flees as one who understands. But if he does not flee it, he is a fornicator and defiled like Esau, and, as one not fleeing Esau but dwelling together with him, he does not become a son of Jacob, who had fled it. […]

27:43.t: But if needs be, let us learn from Rebekah how to make provision so that enmity does not provoke wrath and wrath rush headlong into fratricide. Let Rebekah come—that is, let us put on patience, the good guardian of blamelessness—and let her persuade us not to give in to our anger. Let us withdraw somewhat further, until our anger is softened by time and we are taken by surprise at having forgotten the wrong done us. Therefore patience is not much afraid of exile but readily enters upon it, not so much to avoid the danger to salvation as to escape giving incitement to wrongdoing. The loving mother too endures the absence of her dearly beloved son and purposes to give more to the one whom she has harmed, while still consulting the interests of both, to render the one safe against fratricide and the other blameless of crime.
27:43.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 4, Section 14

27:43.t: We have heard the words of an intemperance that is drunk with bodily desires; let us consider the deeds of true virtue. Virtue needs nothing but the grace of God. It pursues the only and supreme good, and it is content with that only good from which we receive all things but on which we bestow nothing because it has no need of anything, just as David says, "I have said to the Lord, 'You are my Lord, for you have no need of my goods.' " And what does the Lord need, when he abounds in all things and imparts everything to us, while providing all things without deficiency?
27:43.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 4, Section 15

28:11.t: I think this is what Jacob's ladder also signifies, when he fled Esau his brother. 'And he came,' it says, 'to Bethel, and slept there, and put a stone at his head.' See our ascetic; he was fleeing a most cruel man, he was fleeing his brother, and he found help in a stone. That stone is Christ; this stone is a help to those who suffer persecution: but to the unbelieving Jews a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. 'And Jacob saw there,' it says, 'a ladder set up from the earth all the way to heaven; and in heaven,' it says, 'the Lord leaning upon it (epestērigmenon autēi). And he saw,' it says, 'angels ascending and descending.' See what he says. He saw angels climbing up; he saw Paul climbing up. He saw angels descending: Judas the traitor was falling down. He saw angels ascending: holy men going from earth to heaven. He saw angels descending: the devil and the demons and his army cast down headlong from heaven. Great is the difficulty of climbing from earth to the heavenly places. […]

Jacob, at the time when he was fleeing his brother into Mesopotamia, came to Luz: and there, it says, he placed a stone for himself at his head. Under his head the stone was Christ. He never placed a stone at his head, except at the time when he fled his persecutor. When he remained in his father's house, as long as he was in his father's house and had the comforts of the flesh, he did not have a stone at his head. He departed from his home naked, he departed with a staff; and at once, that very night, he found a stone, and placed it at his head. Because he had such a pillow on which to take his rest, see his vision. 'He saw,' it says, 'a ladder reaching from the earth to heaven; and he saw,' it says, 'angels descending and ascending.' He saw angels coming from heaven to earth, and others ascending from earth to the heavens. Do you wish to know that that stone, which was at Jacob's head, was Christ the cornerstone? 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.' […]

This was figured in Jacob’s placing a stone at his head, and so sleeping. The patriarch Jacob had placed a stone at his head: sleeping with that stone at his head, he saw heaven opened, and a ladder from heaven to earth, and Angels ascending and descending; after this vision he awaked, anointed the stone, and departed. In that “stone” he understood Christ; for that reason he anointed it. Take notice what it is whereby Christ is preached. What is the meaning of that anointing of a stone, especially in the case of the Patriarchs who worshipped but One God? It was however done as a figurative act: and he departed. For he did not anoint the stone, and come to worship there constantly, and to perform sacrifice there. It was the expression of a mystery; not the commencement of sacrilege. And notice the meaning of “the stone.” “The Stone which the builders refused, this is become the head of the corner.” Notice here a great mystery. The “Stone” is Christ. […]

The same Jacob, when he was fleeing from Esau his brother, came to a certain place; and when he had put a stone under his head, he slept there. In his sleep he saw a ladder at his head, set up from the earth all the way to heaven, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, and also the angels of God ascending and descending on it (Gen. 28:12). By the stone Christ is understood; indeed our foundation is Christ, of whom the Apostle says: For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus (1 Cor. 3:11). Therefore we place our head upon the stone if, from good works, we build our wall upon Christ.

28:12.t: I would say that the exercise of piety resembles a ladder, that ladder which once the blessed Jacob saw, of which one part was near the earth and reaching to the ground, the other extended above, even to the very heavens. Therefore, those who are being introduced to a life of virtue must place their foot upon the first steps and from there always mount upon the next, until by gradual progress they have ascended to the height attainable by human nature. As withdrawal from the earth is the first step on the ladder, so in a manner of life in harmony with God the departure from evil is the first.

Jacob set out and slept—evidence of tranquility of spirit—and saw angels of God ascending and descending. This means he foresaw Christ on earth; the band of angels was descending to Christ and ascending to him, so as to render service to their rightful master in loving servitude.
28:12.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life, Book 2, Chapter 4, Section 16

28:12.t: For this reason he mounted upon the cross, that he might lift us up from earth on high. I think that this cross of the Savior is the ladder which Jacob saw. On that ladder the angels were descending and ascending; on that ladder, that is, the cross, the Jews descend, and the gentiles ascend.

Degrees are either of ascent or of descent. But degrees, as they are used in this Psalm, are of ascending…There are therefore both those who ascend and those who descend on that ladder. Who are they that ascend? They who progress towards the understanding of things spiritual. Who are they that descend? They who, although, as far as men may, they enjoy the comprehension of things spiritual: nevertheless, descend unto the infants, to say to them such things as they can receive, so that, after being nourished with milk, they may become fitted and strong enough to take spiritual meat…

Jacob saw a ladder in a dream; and on a ladder he saw angels ascending and descending: and he anointed the stone which he had placed at his head. You have heard that the Messias is Christ; you have heard that Christ is the Anointed. For Jacob did not place the stone, the anointed stone, that he might come and adore it: otherwise that would have been idolatry, not a pointing out of Christ. What was done was a pointing out of Christ, so far as it behoved such a pointing out to be made, and it was Christ that was pointed out. A stone was anointed, but not for an idol. A stone anointed; why a stone? "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on Him shall not be confounded." Why anointed? Because Christus comes from chrisma. But what saw he then on the ladder? Ascending and descending angels. So it is the Church, brethren: the angels of God are good preachers, preaching Christ; this is the meaning of, "they ascend and descend upon the Son of man."

Now the Dweller in heaven shewed this ladder aforetime, as in a mystery, to the elect of the Fathers, the blessed Jacob; and also that those who went up and those who came down upon it were angels. And that that ladder belongeth not to heavenly angels alone, the word of the Book indicateth to us, because the angels of God were going up and coming down thereupon; for every man who draweth nigh to enquire thereat, and who beginneth to mount it, laboureth after the order of angels, and is numbered among the elect of spiritual beings, and he hath inscribed his name as a heavenly soldier. And as the children of men who receive human positions, and who labour in some one of the grades of the world, change the name of "rustics", by which they were formerly called, to "servants" (or soldiers), so also the man who of his own freewill enrolleth himself in the company which Christ hath formed, and who serveth in the army of spiritual beings, the word of the Book nameth him "angel", and not "man", and rightly so, because he […]
28:12.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

28:12.t: Now when Jacob, wishing to rest in a certain place, put a stone under his head, he saw in his sleep a ladder standing upon the earth with its top touching heaven. [He saw] also angels of God ascending and descending on it and the Lord resting on the ladder saying to him, "I am the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac." And rising in the morning and rendering praise to the Lord with due trepidation, he took the stone and set it up as a mark, pouring oil on it.The Lord made mention of this place and most clearly bore witness in a figurative way concerning himself and his faithful ones. The ladder which he saw is the church, which has its birth from the earth but its "way of life in heaven," And by it angels ascend and descend, when evangelists announce at one time to perfect hearers the preeminent hidden mysteries of [Christ's] divinity and at another time announce to those still untaught the weaknesses of his humanity. […]

The vision of the ladder agrees with this meaning; for the two larger pieces of wood of the ladder, which are on each side and are raised from the lower parts to the upper, signify the two precepts of love. By the steps, however, which are inserted crosswise on each side into those two pieces of wood, the other virtues are signified. And just as the two pieces of wood cannot be held together without the steps, nor the steps without the two pieces of wood, so love cannot exist without the other virtues, nor the other virtues without love. And just as the various steps, unless they are inserted on each side into the two larger pieces of wood, cannot provide ascent for people, so the other virtues, unless they are born from love of God and love of neighbor, cannot provide ascent for those who wish to go to heaven, as the apostle John says: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 Jn. 4:20). […]

The spiritual senses denote mental perceptions concerning the truth to be contemplated. This contemplation indeed was in the Prophets through revelation with respect to the threefold vision, namely corporeal, imaginative, and intellectual; in other just persons, however, it is found through speculation, which begins from sense and arrives at imagination, and from imagination to reason, from reason to understanding, from understanding to intelligence; from intelligence, however, to wisdom or ecstatic knowledge, which begins here on the way but is consummated in everlasting glory.

And in these degrees consists the ladder of Jacob, whose summit reaches heaven: and the throne of Solomon, upon which sits the most wise King, truly peaceful and loving as the most beautiful bridegroom and wholly desirable: upon whom the Angels desire to gaze, and toward whom the desire of holy souls sighs, as the hart longs for the fountains of waters.

The hierarchical levels are disposed in the soul in a threefold manner: in relation to ascent, to descent, and to the return to God. Then the soul sees "angels of God ascending and descending" upon it; as Jacob saw in his mind.

Since therefore one must first ascend before descending on the ladder of Jacob, let us place the first step of ascent at the bottom, setting this entire sensible world before us as a mirror, through which we may pass over to God, the supreme Artificer, so that we may be true Hebrews passing over from Egypt to the land promised to the Fathers, and also Christians passing over with Christ from this world to the Father, and also lovers of wisdom, who calls and says: Pass over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my generations. For from the greatness of the beauty and of the creature, the Creator of these things can be knowably seen.

These six considerations having therefore been traversed, as if they were the six steps of the throne of the true Solomon, by which one arrives at peace, where the true peaceful one rests in a peaceful mind as in an interior Jerusalem; and as if also the six wings of the Cherub, by which the mind of the true contemplative, filled with the illumination of supernal wisdom, may be borne upward; and as if also the first six days, in which the mind must be exercised, so that it may at last arrive at the sabbath of rest; after our mind has contemplated God outside itself through vestiges and in the vestiges, within itself through the image and in the image, above itself through the similitude of the divine light shining upon us and in that light itself, insofar as is possible according to the state of wayfaring and the exercise of our mind; […]

28:13.t:
Yes, and equally with us they knew and bore witness to the Word of God, Whom we love to call Christ. They were thought worthy in very remarkable ways of beholding His actual presence and theophany.

Remember how Moses calls the Being, Who appeared to the patriarchs, and often delivered to them the oracles afterwards written down in Scripture, sometimes God and Lord, and sometimes the Angel of the Lord. He clearly implies that this was not the Omnipotent God, but a secondary Being, rightly called the God and Lord of holy men, but the Angel of the Most High His Father. Thus he says:

"10. And Jacob went forth ... to Charran, 11. and came to a certain place, and he slept there. . . . And he took of the stones of the place, and put it at his head, and lay down to sleep in that place, 12. and he dreamed: and behold, a ladder fixed on the earth whose top reached to heaven, and the angels of God ascended and descended on it. 13. 28:13.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 5

28:13.t:
[Passage quoted, Gen. xxviii. 10-19.]

THIS Being who here answers him at such length, you will find, if you read on, to be Lord and God, and the Angel of God, from the words Jacob himself says to his wives:

"And the angel of the Lord said to me in sleep, Jacob. And I said, Here am I."

And also:

"I have seen, he says, all that Laban doeth to thee. I am the God, that was seen of thee in the place where thou anointedst the pillar for me, and offeredst prayer to me."

Therefore He that said before, I am the Lord God of Abraham thy Father, and the God of Isaac, to whom godly Jacob raises the pillar, was indeed God and Lord: for we must believe that which He Himself says. Not of course the Almighty, but the Second to Him, Who ministers for His Father among men, and brings His Word. Wherefore Jacob here calls Him an Angel: "The Angel of God said to me, speaking in my sleep, ' I am the God who was seen by thee in this place.' " So the same Being is clearly called the Angel of the Lord, and God and Lord in this place. […]
28:13.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 10

28:14.t: Here indeed we have a wonderful fact, which is not remarked by those few pagans who have remained such,—namely, that this God of the Hebrews who was offended by the conquered, and who was also denied acceptance by the conquerors, is now preached and worshipped among all nations. This is that God of Israel of whom the prophet spake so long time since, when he thus addressed the people of God: "And He who brought thee out, the God of Israel, shall be called (the God) of the whole earth." What was thus prophesied has been brought to pass through the name of the Christ, who comes to men in the form of a descendant of that very Israel who was the grandson of Abraham, with whom the race of the Hebrews began. For it was to this Israel also that it was said, "In thy seed shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed." […]
28:14.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 14

28:16.t: It is an extraordinary statement, but it is none the less true, that the Spirit is frequently spoken of as the place of them that are being sanctified, and it will become evident that even by this figure the Spirit, so far from being degraded, is rather glorified. For words applicable to the body are, for the sake of clearness, frequently transferred in scripture to spiritual conceptions. Accordingly we find the Psalmist, even in reference to God, saying "Be Thou to me a champion God and a strong place to save me" and concerning the Spirit "behold there is place by me, and stand upon a rock." Plainly meaning the place or contemplation in the Spirit wherein, after Moses had entered thither, he was able to see God intelligibly manifested to him. This is the special and peculiar place of true worship; for it is said "Take heed to thyself that thou offer not thy burnt offerings in every place . . . but in the place the Lord thy God shall choose." Now what is a spiritual burnt offering? "The sacrifice of praise." […]

Let us listen also unto the words which Jacob spake in that country in which God was revealed unto him, for from them we may especially see his simplicity: "Verily there is the Lord in this place, and I knew it not." Didst thou think, O simple Jacob, that God was limited only to the country in which thy parents lived, and that He did not reveal Himself or make Himself manifest in every place to those who are worthy of His revelation?
28:16.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

28:18.t: And Jacob dreamed of a lofty ladder and stair of Angels, and in a mystery anointed a pillar—perhaps to signify the Rock that was anointed for our sake—and gave to a place the name of The House of God in honour of Him whom he saw; and wrestled with God in human form; whatever this wrestling of God with man may mean . . . possibly it refers to the comparison of man's virtue with God's; and he bore on his body the marks of the wrestling, setting forth the defeat of the created nature; and for a reward of his reverence he received a change of his name; being named, instead of Jacob, Israel—that great and honourable name. Yet neither he nor any one on his behalf, unto this day, of all the Twelve Tribes who were his children, could boast that he comprehended the whole nature or the pure sight of God.

The stone under Jacob's head is the Lord, upon whom we ought to support ourselves with all our concentration, the more so insofar as it is surely clear to us that without him we can do nothing.Jacob anointed the stone and set it up as a mark, because a true Israelite understands that our Redeemer was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his fellows. From this ointment (that is, chrism) Christ received his name, and the mystery of his incarnation is the mark of our redemption. It is good that when the stone was anointed on the earth and raised up as a mark, the Lord was revealed in heaven, for undoubtedly he appeared in time as a man among men while he remained eternal with God the Father. When death was overcome "he ascended over the heaven of heavens to the east," remaining with us as a mark of our salvation "for all days, up to the consummation of the world." He who transferred the body he had assumed from earth to heaven was the One who filled earth, and heaven as well, with the presence of deity.

28:19.t: And Jacob called the name of that place Bethel, and Ulammaus was the name of the city before. From what he had said above, how terrible is this place: this is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven, he now gives the place a name: and he called it Bethel, that is, house of God; which place was called Luza before, which means 'nut' or ἀμύγδαλον. Hence some ridiculously think that the Hebrew word ulam is the name of the city, though ulam means 'before'. So the order of the reading is this: and he called the name of that place Bethel, and before, Luza was the name of the city. All the ancient Scriptures are full of the word ulam or elem, which signifies nothing other than 'before' or 'formerly', or 'porch' or 'lintel' or 'doorposts'.

28:20.t: Then there is Jacob’s prayer to God: “If thou wilt give me bread to eat and raiment to put on,” not “If thou wilt give luxuries and costly things.” What says Solomon, wisest of men? “Give me neither poverty nor riches, but provide what is necessary and sufficient, lest I be filled and become false and say, Who seeth me? or lest I become poor and steal and use profanely the name of my God.” He thus defines riches as satiety and poverty as complete absence of the necessaries of life; and means by sufficiency having neither a deficiency or superfluity of necessaries. But sufficiency has a different meaning in different cases according to the state of the body and its needs in view of the work to be done. For one man needs food more in quantity and more nourishing on account of his toil, another lighter food suitable in every way to his condition because of his weakness; but all alike need the cheaper and easily procurable kinds.

29:6.t: Rachel: sheep, or seeing the beginning, or vision of wickedness, or seeing God. This, however, comes about according to the diversity of accents and letters, so that names are changed even into contrary meanings.

29:16.t: Moreover, there are two several virtues (or talents) which have been proposed to the mind of man. Of these, the one is the active, and the other the contemplative: the one being that whereby the way is taken, and the other that whereby the goal is reached; the one that by which men labour in order that the heart may be purified to see God, and the other that by which men are disengaged and God is seen. Thus the former of these two virtues is occupied with the precepts for the right exercise of the temporal life, whereas the latter deals with the doctrine of that life which is everlasting. In this way, also, the one operates, the other rests; for the former finds its sphere in the purging of sins, the latter moves in the light of the purged. And thus, again, in this mortal life the one is engaged with the work of a good conversation; while the other subsists rather on faith, and is seen only in the person of the very few, and through the glass darkly, and only in part in a kind of vision of the unchangeable truth. […]
29:16.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 5

29:27.t: Complete therefore the week of this one, and I will give you this one also. After Jacob, deceived by fraud, had taken Leah as his wife in place of Rachel, he is told by his father-in-law Laban to fulfil seven days after the wedding of the elder sister, and so to receive Rachel, for whom he was to serve again for another seven years. It was not, then, as some wrongly suppose, after another seven years that he took Rachel as his wife, but after the seven days of the wedding of his first wife. For there follows: [Gen 29:30] and he went in to Rachel: and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him another seven years.

29:32.t: And she conceived and bore a son and called his name Reuben. For brevity of reading I wish to give the etymologies of the names of all the patriarchs together. And she called he says his name Reuben, saying, Because the Lord has seen my humiliation. Reuben means 'son of vision'.
Ruben [Reuben]: seeing son, or seeing in the midst.

29:33.t: And she conceived he says another son and said, Because the Lord has heard me, in that my husband held me in hatred, and he has given me this one also: and she called his name Simeon. From the fact that she was heard, she gave Simeon his name. For Simeon means 'hearing'.
Symeon [Simeon]: hearing, or name of a dwelling.

29:34.t: Of the third, moreover, there follows: and she conceived again and bore a son and said, Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons: therefore she called his name Levi. Where we read my husband will be at my side, Aquila translated my husband will be joined to me, which in Hebrew is said illaue, and is rendered otherwise by the teachers of the Hebrews, so that they say, "my husband will escort me". That is: I have no doubt of my husband's love for me; he will be my companion in this life, and his love will lead me and escort me all the way to death, for I have borne him three sons.

29:35.t: She conceived and gave birth and bore a son and said, "Now over this I will confess to the Lord", and for that reason she called his name Judah. Judah means 'confession'. So from 'confession' the name of the confessor was given. Yet here confession is taken for thanksgiving or for praise, as often in the psalms, and in the Gospel, I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, that is, I give you thanks, or I glorify you.

30:6.t: And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son: and Rachel said, "The Lord has judged me and has heard my voice and has given me a son"; therefore she called his name Dan. She expressed the cause of the name, so that, from the fact that the Lord had judged her, she gave the son of her handmaid the name of judgment: for Dan means 'judgment'.

30:8.t: And Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son: and Rachel said: "God has made me dwell in a dwelling with my sister, and I have prevailed": and she called his name Naphtali. A cause of the name Naphtali is set out here far different from the one written in the Book of Hebrew Names. Hence Aquila too says συνανέστρεψέν με ὁ θεὸς συναναστροφήν [God has turned me about with a turning], in place of which in the Hebrew it is written neptule eloim neptalti. Hence from 'turning' or from 'comparison', since it sounds both, 'comparison' or 'turning', that is, Naphtali, she gave the son his name.
Neptalim [Naphtali]: he has turned me, or he has enlarged me, or at least he has entwined me.

30:11.t: As for what follows, and Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, bore Jacob a son: and Leah said: "In fortune", and she called his name Gad: where we have set down in fortune, and in Greek it is said ἐν τύχῃ, which can be called 'outcome', in the Hebrew it has bagad, which Aquila renders a girding came, while we can say 'in readiness'. For ba can sound both as the preposition in and as he came. So from outcome or readiness, which is called gad, the son of Zilpah was called Gad.
Gad: temptation, or little robber, or fortune.

30:13.t: There follows: and Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, bore Jacob a second son: and Leah said, Blessed am I, because the women call me blessed, and she called his name Asher, riches. 'Riches', that is, πλοῦτος, has been wrongly added, since the etymology of the name Asher is laid open by the authority of Scripture, which says, Blessed am I, and the women call me blessed, and from the fact that she is called blessed by men, she called her son blessed. So Asher means not 'riches' but 'blessed', at least in the present place. For in others, owing to the ambiguity of the word, riches too can be so called.

30:18.t: And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son, and Leah said, "God has given me my reward, because I gave my handmaid to my husband": and she called his name Issachar. The Seventy translators gave the etymology of this name as est merces (there is a reward). Certainly it must not be supposed, as many wrongly read it by adding a pronoun, that it is written thus, is est merces (he is the reward); rather, the whole name means est merces, there is a reward. For is means est (there is), and sachar merces (reward). And this was so because with her son Reuben's mandrakes she had bought for herself her husband's going in, which was due to Rachel.

Issachar follows, whose name is interpreted as “wages” or “reward.” But we shall see the meaning of this name more clearly if we set forth what his mother Leah said at his birth; for she said: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband” (Gen. 30:18). And therefore she called his name Issachar, that is, “reward.” Our flesh ought to be our maidservant; our husband is our God. We give our maidservant to our husband if we bind our flesh to the service of God, if we compel it to keep watch, to fast, and to abstain, and if we subdue its pleasures. Issachar, therefore, was given to Leah as a reward by God; because to those who tame the flesh, who extinguish vices, that reward is given by God, that they may be enriched with virtues.

30:20.t: There follows: and Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son, and Leah said: "God has endowed me with a good dowry: at this time my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons", and she called his name Zebulun. Where we have set down will dwell with me, and the Seventy translated will love me, in the Hebrew it has iezbuleni. And the sense is: because I have borne Jacob six sons, I am therefore now secure: for my husband will dwell with me. Hence my son too is called 'dwelling'. Wrongly, then, and by force, is Zebulun rendered 'flow of the night' in the Book of Names.
Zabulon [Zebulun]: their dwelling, or his oath, or dwelling of strength, or flowing of night.

30:21.t: And after this she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah. This is rendered 'cause', which the Greeks more expressively call δίκην. For she was the cause of the quarrel at Sicima.

30:24.t: After the sons, the names of the parents too must be set down. Leah means 'toiling', Rachel 'sheep'; whose son Joseph, from the fact that his mother had wished another to be added to her, is called 'increase'.

30:32.t: I will pass through all your flock today; separate from it every spotted and parti-coloured beast, and every beast of one colour among the lambs, and the spotted and parti-coloured among the goats, and it shall be my wage: and my justice shall answer for me tomorrow, when my wage comes before you: everything that is not spotted and parti-coloured among the goats and among the lambs shall be theft with me and so on. In the Seventy translators the sense is greatly confused, and to the present day I have been able to find none of our writers who would set out clearly what is said in this place. You want me, says Jacob, to serve you another seven years as well: do what I ask. Separate all the parti-coloured and spotted, sheep as well as goats, and hand them over into the hands of your sons; and in turn, out of each flock, give me the white and the black beasts, that is, those of one colour. If, then, anything spotted is born of the white and the black, which are of one colour, it shall be mine; […]

30:34.t: Laban gladly seized the option given him and, doing as Jacob asked, set a journey of three days between Jacob and his own sons, so that no trickery might arise from the nearness of the flocks.

30:37.t: The just man Jacob comes in like a hired hand and yet is the master who, in his ministry of preaching the gospel, gathered together a flock that is resplendent in the brilliance of its many signal virtues. Thus, when the flock came to drink, he would set before them in the troughs the bough of storax and walnut and that from the plane tree; those who felt desire for the mysteries of the most blessed Trinity that were prefigured there could engender offspring that were not at all discolored, by conceiving them in a devout mind. Good were the sheep that produced the offspring that were good works and that were not degenerate in holy faith. By the storax is meant the incense and the evening sacrifice that is offered to God the Father in the psalm; by the walnut bough, the priestly gift that is offered by Christ. For this is Aaron's bough, that blossomed when it was set down, and through it the grace of priestly holiness was manifested. […]
30:37.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life

30:37.t: So Jacob devised a new trick and fought with natural art against the nature of the white and the black beasts. For taking three rods, of poplar and of almond and of pomegranate (although the Seventy have rods of storax and of nut and of plane), and stripping them in part, he gave the rods a varied colour, so that wherever he had left the bark on the rod the old colour remained, but where he had taken the bark off, a white colour was laid bare. Jacob therefore kept watch, and at the time when the flocks were mounted, and after the heat of the day went eagerly to drink, he set the parti-coloured rods in the troughs, and letting in the rams and the he-goats, in that very eagerness for drinking he had the sheep and the she-goats mounted, so that from the twofold desire, while they drink eagerly and are mounted by the males, they might conceive offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting from above which they beheld in the mirror of the waters. […]

30:41.t: But in that place where it is written that they might conceive at the rods, and in the Hebrew it has iaeahamena, I cannot express the force of the Hebrew word except by circumlocution. For iaeahamena properly denotes the final heat in coupling, by which the whole body is shaken, and the end is near for one who is consummating pleasure.

And the flocks conceived facing Jacob's rods, the rods which he had set before the flocks in the troughs, that they might conceive at them: and among the late sheep he did not set them. And the late ones became Laban's and the early ones Jacob's. This is not found in the Seventy translators, but in place of 'late' and 'early' they translated something else, I know not what, which does not bear on the sense. But what Scripture says is this: Jacob, prudent and shrewd, kept justice and fairness even in his new art. For if the flocks had produced all the lambs and kids spotted, there was some suspicion of trickery, and the envious Laban would have openly opposed this. So he tempered everything in such a way that he himself would receive the fruit of his labour and Laban would not be stripped entirely. Whenever the sheep and goats were mounted in the first season, because the spring offspring is better, he set the rods before them, so that spotted young would be born. […]

Just as Jacob, again, was not the creator of the colors in the flocks, because he placed the various colored rods for the several mothers, as they drank, to look at in conceiving. Yet neither were the cattle themselves creators of the variety of their own offspring, because the variegated image, impressed through their eyes by the sight of the varied rods, clave to their soul, but could affect the body that was animated by the spirit thus affected only through sympathy with this commingling, so far as to stain with color the tender beginnings of their offspring.
